714011.t: Of uncertain origin. Beekes compares χήρα (khḗra, “widow”), assuming common derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave behind”), with original meaning "unoccupied (left-behind) space".

714070.t: By surface analysis, ψύχω (psū́khō, “to breathe, blow; to cool, chill; to dry”, verb) + -η (-ē, zero grade nominal suffix). The original meaning is thus supposed to have been breath.

714076.t: Uncertain. Could be from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰes- (“to blow”), with cognates including Sanskrit भस्त्रा॑ (bhástrā, “bellows”), अप्सु॑ (ápsu, “without breath”), and Albanian badër.

714036.t: From the root of ψεύδω (pseúdō, “to lie”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).

714090.t: From ὅδε (hóde). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀃 (o /⁠hō⁠/)

714023.t: From ψάλλω (psállō, “to touch sharply, to pluck, to pull, to twitch”) + -τήριον (-tḗrion), from ψάω (psáō, “to touch lightly, to rub”), which acquired the meaning of plucking a harp, and later making music in general.

714016.t: An isolated adverbial formation from χώρα (khṓrā, “space”), initially meaning "in another, separate space or place".

714091.t: Contracted form of ἀοιδή (ăoidḗ), from ἀείδω (ăeídō, “to sing”) + -η (-ē).

714056.t: Of unknown origin; possibly related to ψάω (psáō, “to rub, wipe”), and thus of Pre-Greek origin, though the morphology remains unclear if indeed related.

714052.t: Traditionally considered related to ψάω (psáō, “to rub smooth, crumble”), though the morphological function of -φ- (-ph-) would be unclear.

714055.t: If it dissimilated from *ψυθυρ-, it may belong to ψύθος (psúthos, “lie, untruth”). On the other hand, it can be compared to ψίζομαι (psízomai, “to weep”).

714081.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ō. Cognate with Latin ō̆.

714021.t: Unknown; probably Pre-Greek. More at ψάω (psā́ō).

714079.t: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of ψάω (psā́ō, “to rub, wipe”), ψωμός (psōmós, “morsel, bit”), ψωλός (psōlós, “circumcised”), ψωρός (psōrós, “itchy; mangy”) and ψωχός (psōkhós, “sandy”).

714045.t: No convincing Indo-European etymology; probably from Pre-Greek, as evidenced by the irregular alternation between /d/ and /tʰ/ in related terms, the latter in e.g. ψύθος (psúthos, “lie, untruth”), ψυθῶνες (psuthônes, “slanderers”) and the Homeric aorist…

714064.t: Unknown. Like ψεῦδος (pseûdos) and ψύθος (psŭ́thos), it may originally be onomatopoeic and somehow belong with the interjection ψό (psó).

714020.t: Uncertain but perhaps related to ψάλιον (psálion, “curb chain”) and ψέλιον (psélion, “armlet”). Maybe from Pre-Greek.

714034.t: With ψάλιον (psálion, “curb-chain”) and ψαλόν (psalón, “bridle”) an Iranian borrowing.

714058.t: The word is related to similar words meaning "foxes", like ψειαί (pseiaí), ψίαι (psíai), φοῦαι (phoûai) and φύλλες (phúlles). These variations cannot be all understood in Indo-European terms.

714078.t: Traditionally compared to Sanskrit प्साति (psā́ti, “to eat, consume”).

714047.t: Analyzed by Fick as a univerbation from the aorist form of ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck, pull, twitch”) (the ultimate source of psalm) and ἀφάω (apháō, “to handle”). It remains unclear, however, why the aorist was preferred.

714049.t: Verbal adjective, from ψηλαφάω (psēlăphắō, “to feel, grope”) + -τός (-tós).
